newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: World's doctors adopt strong human rights stance.
newsitem.headline: World's doctors adopt strong human rights stance.

text.p: The influential World Medical Association (WMA) on Friday denounced Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and vowed to help free a Nigerian doctor jailed for his political opposition to the military government there.

The WMA 48th general assembly, meeting in South Africa, adopted strong human rights declarations which also bound delegates from 63 member countries to prevent advances in medical technology from being abused by the weapons industry.

Disassociating the medical profession from Karadzic, a hospital psychiatrist in pre-war Sarajevo, for his refusal to appear before the International Criminal Tribunal for War Crimes in the former Yugoslavia, the WMA unanimously adopted a declaration censuring him.
"As a physician he is bringing our profession into disrepute. The WMA denounces Dr Karadzic for not surrendering himself...and demands that he does this forthwith," the assembly resolved.
Karadzic has been indicted with war crimes.
The British Medical Association asked the WMA to ensure that physicians fleeing prosecution for human rights crimes did not register in other countries.

"If doctors are accused of participation in torture, war crimes or crimes against humanity, we should ensure they have no option of walking away and setting up practice elsewhere," BMA head of ethics Vivienne Nathanson urged.

The WMA Secretariat also pledged to request clemency for Nigerian doctor and human rights activist Beko Ransome-Kuti, who was imprisoned for 15 years after a secret trial by a special military tribunal.
The Nigerian Medical Association's Boniface Oye-Adeniran, appealing for WMA assistance, told the assembly its officials had been denied permission to see Ransome-Kuti, formerly its secretary general.
"We're not sure about his state of mind or...health because we have not been able to see him," Oye-Adeniran said.
Delegates also resolved that the medical profession should support international efforts to define criteria that would measure the effects of weapons.
